conversations.question: Explain how a black hole bends light around it

frames.question: Explain how a black hole bends light around it
frames.narration: Black holes are so dense they warp the very fabric of space, forcing light to follow curved paths instead of traveling in a straight line. This effect, called gravitational lensing, creates the iconic glowing ring you see in images of black holes.

spec.title: Gravitational Lensing: How Black Holes Bend Light
spec.sub: General relativity in action: mass curves spacetime.
spec.opener: Black holes are so dense they warp the very fabric of space, forcing light to follow curved paths instead of traveling in a straight line. This effect, called gravitational lensing, creates the iconic glowing ring you see in images of black holes.

props.title: The core principle
props.summary: Massive objects like black holes create a 'gravity well' that curves spacetime. Light, which always follows the shortest path, must follow these curves, resulting in bent trajectories.

blocks.note: Light doesn't actually 'bend' because of gravity's pull on the photons themselves; it follows the curvature of space created by the black hole's immense mass.

props.title: Spacetime curvature near a singularity
props.footer: The arrows represent the slope of spacetime; light follows the path of least resistance through this warped grid.

blocks.note: This vector field shows how space is distorted near a massive object, forcing light to deviate from a straight line.

props.note: The term 'lens' comes from the Latin word for lentil, describing the shape of glass lenses that also bend light.

blocks.note: The term 'lens' comes from the Latin word for lentil, describing the shape of glass lenses that also bend light.

props.title: Observational Proof
props.claim: Light from distant stars is visibly bent by massive objects.

items.text: 1919 Solar Eclipse: Eddington confirmed starlight shifted position near the Sun.
Event Horizon Telescope: Captured the 'shadow' of M87* with a bright photon ring.

blocks.note: We don't just theorize this; we have observed it directly during solar eclipses and through modern radio telescopes.

conversations.question: Explain how OAuth login works, step by step

frames.question: Explain how OAuth login works, step by step
frames.narration: OAuth is the standard way apps let you log in using another service, like Google or GitHub, without ever sharing your actual password. It works by trading temporary digital keys, keeping your credentials safe behind the scenes.

tour.say: OAuth is all about tokens, not passwords. It's the secure way to let apps verify your identity without ever seeing your credentials.
The flow is a five-step handshake. The app asks for permission, you log in with the provider, and the app gets a code to trade for a token.
This is what that exchange looks like in code: the app sends the code and its secret, and the provider hands back the access token.

spec.title: OAuth 2.0: How it Works
spec.sub: The secure handshake between your app, the user, and the identity provider.
spec.opener: OAuth is the standard way apps let you log in using another service, like Google or GitHub, without ever sharing your actual password. It works by trading temporary digital keys, keeping your credentials safe behind the scenes.

props.title: The Core Concept
props.summary: OAuth 2.0 uses 'tokens' instead of passwords. The app asks the identity provider (like Google) for permission, and the provider gives a temporary key that the app uses to prove who you are.

blocks.note: Think of it like a hotel key card: you don't get the master key to the whole building, just a temporary pass that lets you into your specific room.

steps.detail: The app redirects your browser to the identity provider's login page.
You enter your credentials directly on the provider's site, not the app's.
The provider sends a short-lived code back to the app's redirect URL.

steps.action: App exchanges code for Access Token
steps.detail: The app sends the code + its secret key to the provider's server.
The provider verifies the app and code, then issues an Access Token.

blocks.note: This five-step dance ensures the app never sees your password, only the token the provider gives them.

lines.text: App sends the auth code to the provider to get the token
Provider responds with the access token

blocks.note: This is the critical moment: the app trades the temporary code for a secure token that acts as your digital ID.

rows.t: Client ID: Public identifier for the app
Client Secret: Private key known only to app and provider
Redirect URI: Where the provider sends the user back
Access Token: The temporary key used for API calls

blocks.note: These four pieces are the building blocks of every secure OAuth connection.

frames.question: How does a neural network learn? Walk me through it as a labeled diagram
frames.narration: Neural networks learn by adjusting their internal weights to minimize error. It's a cycle of guessing, measuring how wrong the guess was, and then nudging the connections to get closer to the right answer next time.

tour.say: The process is a continuous loop: forward pass for prediction, then backpropagation to fix the errors.
You can see the model getting smarter as the training loss drops steadily over twenty epochs.

spec.title: How a Neural Network Learns
spec.sub: From random guesses to accurate predictions through backpropagation.
spec.opener: Neural networks learn by adjusting their internal weights to minimize error. It's a cycle of guessing, measuring how wrong the guess was, and then nudging the connections to get closer to the right answer next time.

props.title: The Learning Loop
props.summary: The network repeatedly passes data forward, calculates error, and adjusts weights backward to improve accuracy.

blocks.note: Learning is an iterative process of refining connections, moving from raw, random guesses toward high-precision output.

stages.caption: Data flows through layers to produce a prediction.

stages.label: Loss Calculation
stages.caption: Compare the prediction to the actual target.

stages.label: Backpropagation
stages.caption: Calculate how each weight contributed to the error.

stages.label: Weight Update
stages.caption: Adjust weights slightly to reduce future error.

blocks.note: This loop repeats thousands of times, with the network learning a little bit more with every single pass.

props.title: Training Progress
props.footer: Loss drops as the model converges on the optimal weight configuration.

blocks.note: As training continues, the loss curve trends downward, showing the model is successfully minimizing its mistakes.

items: Weights: The strength of connections between neurons.

Gradient Descent: The optimization algorithm used to find the best weights.

props.title: The 15-Minute Rule
props.summary: Shift your bedtime and wake-up time by exactly 15 minutes each day. This gradual approach minimizes 'social jetlag' and helps your body adjust without the crash.

blocks.note: Consistency is the secret; shifting by 15 minutes daily is gentle enough to avoid the exhaustion of a sudden, drastic change.

steps.detail: Get 15-30 minutes of direct sunlight within 30 minutes of waking. This is the strongest signal to your brain to stop melatonin production.
Move your bedtime and wake-up time 15 minutes earlier or later each day until you hit your target window.
Stop all caffeine intake at least 8-10 hours before your target bedtime to ensure your sleep pressure builds naturally.

blocks.note: These three habits—morning light, gradual shifts, and caffeine timing—are the pillars of resetting your biological clock.

events.title: Initial Adjustment
events.detail: Shift your schedule by 15 minutes daily. Expect some grogginess; stay consistent with morning light.

events.title: The Mid-Point
events.detail: Continue the 15-minute increments. Avoid naps longer than 20 minutes to keep your sleep drive high.

events.title: Stabilization
events.detail: Lock in your target times. Keep the same wake-up time even on weekends to cement the new rhythm.

blocks.note: This timeline breaks your two-week reset into three phases: initial adjustment, mid-point momentum, and final stabilization.

spec.title: The Krebs Cycle: Energy Production
spec.sub: A step-by-step breakdown of the citric acid cycle.
spec.opener: The Krebs cycle is the heart of cellular respiration, turning fuel into energy. It's a continuous loop that processes carbon molecules to power your cells.

props.title: What is the Krebs cycle?
props.summary: A series of chemical reactions used by all aerobic organisms to release stored energy through the oxidation of acetyl-CoA derived from carbohydrates, fats, and proteins.

blocks.note: The cycle is a closed loop of eight enzymatic steps that extract high-energy electrons from carbon fuels.

props.title: Energy yield per turn
props.footer: Each turn produces high-energy electron carriers for the electron transport chain.

blocks.note: For every molecule of acetyl-CoA, the cycle generates three NADH, one FADH2, and one ATP.

events.title: Citrate Formation
events.detail: Acetyl-CoA joins oxaloacetate.

events.title: Carbon Loss
events.detail: Two CO2 molecules are released.

events.title: ATP Synthesis
events.detail: Substrate-level phosphorylation.

events.title: Regeneration
events.detail: Oxaloacetate is reformed.

blocks.note: The cycle begins by combining a two-carbon unit with a four-carbon acceptor, then stripping carbons until the acceptor is restored.

props.title: Metabolic significance
props.question: Why is the cycle central to metabolism?
findings: Provides precursors for amino acid synthesis.
Links carbohydrate, fat, and protein metabolism.
Primary source of electrons for ATP production.
props.conclusion: It is the metabolic hub of the cell, balancing energy production with biosynthetic needs.

blocks.note: Beyond energy, the cycle acts as a crossroads for building the molecules your body needs.
